overview: Timur established his power in Transoxiana in 1370 and made Samarkand his capital. His conquests created a vast but unstable empire; after his death in 1405, descendants governed changing territories and rival courts. The imported 1400 to 1492 polygon cannot show those shifts and greatly overstates continuous control across that whole period. It also stops before the loss of Herat in 1507. This card distinguishes Timur’s conquests from the later communities and courts that inherited his dynasty’s name.

periods.title: Timur’s conquests
periods.summary: Samarkand became the centre of an expanding military empire.

periods.title: Successors and regional courts
periods.summary: Timurid rulers maintained influential courts while their territories fragmented.

items.text: Timur’s campaigns devastated many towns and displaced people through killing, enslavement and forced relocation. Skilled artisans were taken to Samarkand, enriching the capital while damaging workshops elsewhere. Later rulers rebuilt parts of the economy. The monuments and beautiful objects that survive belong alongside this harder history of families losing homes, livelihoods and freedom.

Gowhar-Shad, Shah Rukh’s wife and the mother of Ulugh Beg and Baisunghur, played an active role in politics and public building. She commissioned a major mosque at Mashhad, completed in 1418, and a mosque and college complex at Herat. Her influence ran through family relationships, court allies and foundations that supported institutions beyond her own household.

Farming paid much of the state’s bills. Under Shah Rukh, damaged irrigation in the Marv oasis was repaired to restore production. Fifteenth-century histories and a later agricultural manual describe cereals, legumes, vegetables, fruit, nuts and flowers in the wider Khorasan region. The food supply depended on farmers, water management and seasonal work as much as on royal decisions.

Around Herat, the Juy-e Soltani canal was dug on Abu Sa‘id’s orders in 1467 to 1469. It improved irrigation for agricultural districts on both sides of the river south of the city. Water also helped extend gardens and leisure grounds. A canal could help grow dinner and create a pleasant place to spend an afternoon, although access and benefits were unequal.

Shah Rukh’s government restored and enlarged Herat’s bazaar and promoted manufacturing and trade. Towns were places where settled farmers and craftspeople exchanged goods with pastoral communities. Long-distance caravans also carried valuable products such as silk and porcelain between Central Asian and Iranian centres and India and China. Market life connected very different ways of making a living.

The poet and statesman Ali Shir Navai supported a complex at Herat with a college, a Sufi meeting and residential institution, a hospital and a bathhouse. Its kitchen also fed people in need. Teaching, worship, healthcare, washing and food could therefore be supported within one network of charitable buildings. This was a particular endowed foundation, rather than a service available equally everywhere.

A manuscript painted at Herat in 1431 or 1432 shows the storybook lovers Laila and Majnun meeting as children at a mosque school. Colourful tiles, patterned surfaces, writing and figures fill the page. Commissioned for Prince Baisunghur, it shows how an older Persian poem could become an elaborate illustrated book. Its classroom is a literary scene, not a survey of every child’s schooling.

A workshop progress report from around 1430, attributed to Ja‘far al-Tabrizi at Baisunghur’s court, tracks the work of several kinds of makers. It mentions book illustrators, illuminators and binders alongside stonecutters, tent-makers and people supplying designs for saddles. A royal library could be a busy production centre. Beautiful books emerged from coordinated labour, with plenty of unfinished jobs to report.

Ulugh Beg’s observatory at Samarkand used a huge measuring instrument with a radius of about forty metres, partly set below ground. Astronomers including al-Kashi, Qadi-zada and Ali Qushji worked on observations and calculations. Their programme checked and corrected the positions of more than a thousand stars. This was a team achievement built from careful measuring, calculation and comparison.

Al-Kashi’s letters to his father describe Ulugh Beg joining scholarly discussions and taking an interest in appointments. One report has the ruler performing difficult astronomical calculations while riding a horse. We cannot watch the ride ourselves, but the letter preserves a memorable contemporary claim. Mathematics at this court involved conversation and teaching as well as impressive instruments.

A copper coin of Shah Rukh, Ashmolean HCR16074, begins its inscription “السلطان الاعظم”, meaning “the supreme sultan”. The museum dates it broadly to 1405 to 1446 and identifies the mint as Ta’us. This is Arabic language in Arabic script, transcribed here in modern type. Such titles proclaimed authority; they do not establish which language everyone spoke at home.

Ulugh Beg owned a white jade jug now in the Gulbenkian Museum. Its dragon-shaped handle was made separately and attached with gold rivets; specialists disagree about whether that handle was original or added later. Later Mughal owners added their own inscriptions. One treasured vessel can therefore carry several centuries of ownership, alterations and claims to an illustrious family past.

A glazed bowl dated 1419 or 1420 carries a repeated Persian blessing that the museum translates as wishing for a good outcome or good fortune. A spread-winged bird fills its centre, while lotus leaves run around the outside. The maker used lustre decoration on stonepaste. Even a vessel’s decoration could combine a kindly wish with a display of skilled craftsmanship.

ending.text: The empire broke into competing territories rather than falling everywhere at once. In 1507, Muhammad Shaybani’s forces took Herat, ending its Timurid court; some former officials continued serving under the new rulers. The dynasty’s descendants and cultural traditions survived. Babur, a descendant of Timur, founded Mughal rule in India in 1526. The map’s 1492 cutoff is therefore a coverage boundary, not the dynasty’s disappearance.
